mcqs.question: Your ISP upgrades you from a copper DSL line to fiber. Why doesn't this require any change to your browser or the websites you visit?
options: Because HTTP servers negotiate the physical medium during the TLS handshake
Because browsers auto-detect the physical medium and recompile their networking code at runtime
Because fiber and copper both use the exact same electrical signaling standard
Because layering means the physical/link layer can change independently as long as it still hands IP packets up through the same interface
mcqs.explanation: Layering's whole point is that swapping the link-layer technology doesn't touch layers above it, since the interface (handing packets to IP) stays the same. Fiber and copper use completely different signaling (the same-signaling claim is false), and neither browsers nor TLS negotiate physical media (the browser-auto-recompile and TLS-handshake-negotiation claims describe things that don't happen).

mcqs.question: Why does the real internet run on TCP/IP rather than the OSI model, even though OSI is taught first?
options: TCP/IP shipped as working, deployed code on the early internet while OSI was still being finalized as a standard, so the industry built around what already worked
TCP/IP has fewer layers, which makes it inherently faster at moving bits
OSI is technically incapable of routing packets across autonomous systems
OSI was designed only for LANs and cannot address hosts across a WAN
mcqs.explanation: This is a history-of-technology fact, not a technical limitation: TCP/IP won because it was already running and adopted before OSI's standardization process finished. Layer count has no bearing on raw speed, and OSI was never limited to LANs — it's a general reference model.

mcqs.question: A colleague says "the router dropped the frame due to a routing table miss." What's imprecise about this statement?
options: Nothing — routers operate on frames just like switches do
Routers operate on packets (network layer); "frame" is the data-link PDU that a switch, not a router, would drop
Routing table misses never cause drops, only ARP misses do
"Frame" and "packet" are fully interchangeable terms in networking
mcqs.explanation: A router makes forwarding decisions on packets (layer 3, IP-addressed); it strips the incoming frame's link-layer header first. Calling the dropped unit a "frame" misattributes the PDU to the wrong layer — precise PDU vocabulary is exactly what this concept teaches.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks "which OSI layer handles TLS encryption?" What's the best way to think about this question?
options: Find the literal kernel module named 'presentation layer' and report which layer it's compiled into
Refuse to answer since TLS runs over TCP/IP, not OSI, so the question is malformed
Classify TLS's responsibility (encoding/encrypting data) against OSI's conceptual layers — it maps to Presentation (6), even though no OS literally implements a separate Presentation module
Say TLS operates at every layer simultaneously since encryption affects the whole stack
mcqs.explanation: OSI is a conceptual model for classifying responsibilities, not a literal implementation — so the right move is to map TLS's job (encoding/encryption) onto the layer whose job matches, which is Presentation. Refusing to answer or claiming 'every layer' both miss that OSI is still useful as a classification tool even though TCP/IP is what's actually running.
